{{About|an algebraic differential equation with an universality property|universal differential equation in physics-informed machine learning|Neural differential equation}}
{{technical|date=May 2025}}

A '''universal differential equation''' ('''UDE''') is a non-trivial [[differential algebraic equation]] with the property that its solutions can [[Approximation theory|approximate]] any [[continuous function]] on any interval of the real line to any desired level of accuracy.

Precisely, a (possibly implicit) differential equation <math>P(y', y'', y''', ..., y^{(n)}) = 0</math> is a UDE if for any continuous real-valued function <math>f</math> and for any positive continuous function <math> \varepsilon </math> there exist a [[Smooth function|smooth]] solution <math> y</math> of <math>P(y', y'', y''', ..., y^{(n)}) = 0</math> with  <math> |y(x) - f(x)| < \varepsilon (x) </math> for all <math> x \in \R </math>.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Rubel |first=Lee A. |date=1981 |title=A universal differential equation |url=https://www.ams.org/bull/1981-04-03/S0273-0979-1981-14910-7/ |journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=4 |issue=3 |pages=345–349 |doi=10.1090/S0273-0979-1981-14910-7 |issn=0273-0979|doi-access=free }}</ref>

The existence of an UDE has been initially regarded as an analogue of the [[universal Turing machine]] for analog computers, because of a result of Shannon that identifies the outputs of the [[general purpose analog computer]] with the solutions of algebraic differential equations.<ref name=":0" /> However, in contrast to universal Turing machines, UDEs do not dictate the evolution of a system, but rather sets out certain conditions that any evolution must fulfill.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Pouly |first1=Amaury |last2=Bournez |first2=Olivier |date=2020-02-28 |title=A Universal Ordinary Differential Equation |url=https://lmcs.episciences.org/6168/pdf |journal=Logical Methods in Computer Science |volume=16| issue = 1 |article-number=4437 |arxiv=1702.08328 |doi=10.23638/LMCS-16(1:28)2020|s2cid=4736209 }}</ref>

== Examples ==

* Rubel found the first known UDE in 1981. It is given by the following implicit differential equation of fourth-order:<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> <math>3 y^{\prime 4} y^{\prime \prime} y^{\prime \prime \prime \prime 2}-4 y^{\prime 4} y^{\prime \prime \prime 2} y^{\prime \prime \prime \prime}+6 y^{\prime 3} y^{\prime \prime 2} y^{\prime \prime \prime} y^{\prime \prime \prime \prime}+24 y^{\prime 2} y^{\prime \prime 4} y^{\prime \prime \prime \prime}-12 y^{\prime 3} y^{\prime \prime} y^{\prime \prime \prime 3}-29 y^{\prime 2} y^{\prime \prime 3} y^{\prime \prime \prime 2}+12 y^{\prime \prime 7}=0</math>
* Duffin obtained a family of UDEs given by:<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Duffin |first=R. J. |date=1981 |title=Rubel's universal differential equation |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=78 |issue=8 |pages=4661–4662 |doi=10.1073/pnas.78.8.4661 |pmid=16593068 |pmc=320216 |bibcode=1981PNAS...78.4661D |issn=0027-8424|doi-access=free}}</ref>
:<math>n^2 y^{\prime \prime \prime \prime} y^{\prime 2}+3 n(1-n) y^{\prime \prime \prime} y^{\prime \prime} y^{\prime}+\left(2 n^2-3 n+1\right) y^{\prime \prime 3}=0</math> and <math>n y^{\prime \prime \prime \prime} y^{\prime 2}+(2-3 n) y^{\prime \prime \prime} y^{\prime \prime} y^{\prime}+2(n-1) y^{\prime \prime 3}=0</math>,  whose solutions are of class '''''<math>C^n</math>''''' for ''n'' > 3.

* Briggs proposed another family of UDEs whose construction is based on [[Jacobi elliptic functions]]:<ref>{{cite arXiv |last=Briggs |first=Keith |date=2002-11-08 |title=Another universal differential equation |eprint=math/0211142 }}</ref>
:<math>y^{\prime \prime \prime \prime} y^{\prime 2}-3 y^{\prime \prime \prime \prime} y^{\prime \prime} y^{\prime}+2\left(1-n^{-2}\right) y^{\prime \prime 3}=0</math>, where ''n'' > 3.

* Bournez and Pouly proved the existence of a fixed polynomial vector field ''p'' such that for any ''f'' and ''ε'' there exists some initial condition of the differential equation y' = p(y) that yields a unique and analytic solution satisfying  |''y''(''x'') − ''f''(''x'')| < ''ε''(''x'') for all ''x'' in '''R'''.<ref name=":1" />
